frontiers.title: The proposed Webb line toward England
frontiers.summary: A 1773 Saybrook/Chester church-record transcript establishes a James Webb–Elizabeth Douglas marriage in the relevant locality, but the couple is not yet connected directly to James Webb Jr. and both identities remain unresolved.
frontiers.heroAlt: Approved Webb proof-boundary composition with faded England and Grand Union flag context
evidenceFor: Dedicated Webb family histories repeatedly identify another James Webb and an Elizabeth Douglas as James Webb Jr.'s parents.
A published transcript of the surviving Third Church of Saybrook, now Chester, entries records the marriage of James Webb and Elizabeth Douglas on 9 December 1773.
The 1790 federal census places a James Webb household in Saybrook among a broader Webb and Douglass locality cluster.
The reported father-name is consistent enough to remain a strong research lead rather than a discarded tree hint.
The proposed deeper chain contains real documented New England people who can be tested against land, probate, church and kinship records.
limitsAndConflicts: No decisive original town, church, land or probate record currently links James Webb Jr. to the reported parent couple.
The 1773 marriage proves that a namesake couple existed together; it does not prove that they were James Jr.'s parents.
Conflicting compiled profiles assign the elder James incompatible birth and death years, including 1733–1817 and 1754–1823.
Compiled material appears to combine two women named Elizabeth Douglas, producing conflicting dates and identities.
The surviving East Hampton Congregational register has a gap in the relevant period; the missing baptism is not evidence against the relationship.
The Gideon Webb, older New England and English links remain uncorrelated compiled genealogy, not established descent.

candidatePaths.warning: Candidate parents, not established ancestors; Elizabeth Douglas may combine two different women.
Compiled New England chain requiring original parish, land, probate and kinship evidence.
Proposed English extension; identity and migration chain remain unresolved.

frontiers.nextProof: Retrieve and abstract the Saybrook District James Webb probate packet, then correlate Chester/Saybrook, Chatham/East Hampton and western-New-York church, land, tax, household and sibling evidence before evaluating the deeper New England and English chain.

frontiers.title: The Gooley, Goulet and possible French connection
frontiers.summary: John Peter Gooley's Canadian birth is strongly supported, but his reported father Peter or Pierre has not been identified securely.
evidenceFor: John Peter Gooley consistently appears in later records as Canadian-born.
The Gooley or Gouley surname provides a legitimate lead for Canadian parish and civil-record research.
A Pierre Goulet and Louise-Anne Tellier marriage is documented in Quebec in 1846 and can be tested as a candidate family.
limitsAndConflicts: No baptism or equivalent direct record has yet named John Peter Gooley's parents.
The spelling resemblance among Gooley, Gouley and Goulet does not prove that the families are identical.
Irish, Anglophone and French-Canadian origins remain open possibilities.
The documented 1846 Goulet marriage has not been connected to John Peter Gooley.

candidatePaths.warning: Reported parent and origin question; Irish, Anglophone and French-Canadian possibilities remain open.
The 1846 Pierre Goulet–Louise-Anne Tellier marriage is authentic, but no record yet identifies that Pierre as John Peter Gooley's father.

frontiers.nextProof: Find John Peter Gooley's baptism or another direct record naming his parents before connecting the documented candidate Goulet family or extending the line toward France.
